projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Harvey Parry was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- where you went to school, where you first heard about Pearl Harbor or where you were Pearl Harbor day, if you remember that, and then how you got into the service. And tell me a little about your dad and the rest of your family being in the service. And then just tell the story, and then we'll go on from there.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay? Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: My name is Harvey Pearson Parry, Jr. I was born in Groveville, New Jersey, September 24th, 1925. And I forget what the heck you said.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And just tell me -- I live in Wilmington, Delaware.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: I said that, didn't I?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No. You were born in --

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Oh, I live in Wilmington, Delaware, now. I went to school at Bancroft School, graduate out of there in September -- or June of '42 and went to Brown Vocational School. And that was the year I got called back in the -- I was -- I went -- enlisted in the service. Is that all coming out like --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah, you're fine.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me about your recollections of Pearl Harbor day, if you remember it.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, Pearl Harbor day, I remember most of it. It got me a little worried because my father was in the service then -- in the service then. He enlisted in 1939. And that's when I was, like, worried about him, where he was. We didn't know where he was stationed at or anything. So in 1942, September 24th, my birthday, 17th birthday, I enlisted in the Navy. And from there I went to boot camp, Rhode Island, Connecticut -- Rhode Island, New Port, Rhode Island, and stayed 30 days there. From there I went down to Bainbridge, Maryland. And they needed 1,500 Seaman Second. From there I went to amphibious training down Little Creek, Virginia, in landing craft boats. And that's when they made me like a coxswain, which is a captain of it. The boat is 36 feet long, carries 36 troops in there to the beach. And then from there I went further training down in Fort Pierce, Florida, and stayed there while more amphibious training and swimming. And from there I went aboard the ship in 1943, the USS Elmore APA thirty -- 42. I try to get that mixed up with my other one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So your first -- What was your first basic battle, where you went. Tell me a little bit about where you went. Where was the Elmore when you loaded on, and then where did you go from there, and what were your assignments?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Okay. When I went aboard the ship at USS Elmore, it was in Baltimore, Maryland. From there, we left and went through the Panama Canal up to San Diego, California. That's where we did some training with the Marines out there and then took them aboard our ship. And from there we went to -- stopped off at Pearl Harbor out there. And the next morning when you woke up, you saw all the battleships, aircraft carriers with us, so we knew we were going to an invasion. And that's where we went to Eniwetok Atoll, called the Roi-Namur. And I was in the first wave, then went in the beach there, and that was my first invasion I made. I was 18 years old then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you were a coxswain?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yes, coxswain. You was like the captain of that boat. You had to do -- wear a -- I skipped somewhere. I went to navigation pilot school in Little Creek, Virginia, when I was there. And that's what you had to know about that to make sure you got the troops in the beach at the right place.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you have any protection at all?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: No, just our life jacket, and we didn't carry no sidearms. All we had was two 30mm guns on the stern of the boat that we had.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How big was your crew?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Four, myself and three other crew. I had a bow hook man, signalman, and a motor mach who took care of the motors for us. And that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So what happened with this first battle you went into? What were you feeling about? What were you thinking and --

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, I wasn't scared then because I was, like, you know, 17. I was seeing the world. I thought this was great. Then all of a sudden you seen something hit the water when you's going in, and that's when I stooped down a little farther. I had a helmet on. That's when I started getting scared and worried, you know. But you had to stay up a little bit so you could see the beach where you was going, you know. So then after that I really got a little scared each invasion I made, which in the time I made about seven invasions. And I can't count on my fingers how many air attacks and submarine attacks the ships had during the course of the invasion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What would the troops feel when they went into the beach? I mean, did you --

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, I, first, when -- I had to feel a little sorry for them, because once you're going aboard ship, you got seasick. And once they got over that motion on there, they got cured of it. But when they went into the landing craft, they had different motion on there. Then they got sick on there again. And I really felt sorry for them, because here they're going to fight a battle, and you drop them off at the beach, you know. And they were scared too. They were all young like I was in there. And then one time I asked the guy, I said, "What are you standing back here with a machine gun for?" He said, "If they don't go in, I kill them." I said, "Well, who's going to take care of you if you don't, you know?" But that never happened in all my invasions. Them guys just run off that boat and into the battle.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: He said he actually -- that was his duty?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah. That's what his duty was, that none of them refused to get off of there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah. And that never happened, no more. I mean, they guys got off of there. They were brave. They didn't have to -- Nobody had to tell them or push them off.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did that surprise you?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Oh, yeah. That surprised me when he gave me that answer, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You don't think he was just kidding with you?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: He could have been. I don't know. But he looked serious to me at the time, you know, going in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How many men did you have in that landing craft?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: It would be 36 in there, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, it was a wood -- Tell me about the craft a little bit.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, the craft was just like all pressed plywood. It had, I think, a quarter inch metal on the both sides of it, but that wouldn't stop nothing on it, you know. It was all wooden, you know, except the ramp that went down. That was metal, too, when you -- But that was it. It was just a wooden roll ramp.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What kind of engine did it have? Did it have a --

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Oh, you got me on that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was it single screw?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah, one -- Yeah. And then a lot of times -- The bottom was wooden, I know, because if you hit the coral, you'd punch a hole in your boat, you know, or damage the shaft to the prop, you know, and everything on there. So it wasn't much to take care of you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How far up on the beach did you get to go? Did you push up pretty far?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, different islands you made -- At Eniwetok Atoll there, you got right up on the beach. But some of them you had to go through canals, channels, because of the coral reef you couldn't get through, or if you hit it too hard, you'd punch a hole in there. It's all according to how the tide was laying. They tried to make it perfect so you'd get in, but sometimes you had to hit the sandbar, and they'd have to go maybe 50, 60 feet into the beach wading in that water, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How many trips did you make per --

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, due to -- You went back, and you got stuff like food, ammunition, and things like that. So it's kind of hard to count, because if you had ammunition or whatever, they needed fuel, they took you in the beach right away. But if you had food, you may lay out there two or three hours before you got called in. It's all according to what essential stuff they needed in that beach to take care of the troops.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, were you being shot at?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Not then, that -- The Marines had pushed them back in the beach a good ways, you know, then. But you'd hear bullets back in there firing. And then, like, there at the Marshalls, they got pushed back almost to the beach that time. But I was back aboard ship and getting loaded up for another trip in, you know, when they got pushed back. But they took care of it. At the Marshalls there is, like, they found out later when the tide went out, the Japanese could wade from island to island and reinforce it. That was where the airbase was, and that's what they did. And they didn't know they were doing it for a while. But I'll say the Marines did their job there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you feel that you were part of the Marines or the Navy? I mean, did you feel pretty close to those guys?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Oh, yeah, you felt close to them, for what they had to do. And then you met a lot of them aboard ship. You figure you left in San Diego, and it took you maybe four or five days to get to Hawaii, and I can't remember how long to the islands, but you got to know a lot of them. They did exercises aboard the ship. They cleaned their guns constantly, you know. You got to talk to a lot of them down in the mess hall and things like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And what was your standard day like, since you had your boat, right? Were you assigned your own boat basically?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah. I had boat PA -- mine was 15. That was my boat for the whole time I was there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And what was your -- When you were -- When you weren't dropping troops off, what was your standard day like along, you know -- When you were coming over from San Diego to Hawaii, what was your normal day like?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, mine was you had to stand watches with the ship's company. And we had carried 36 landing craft boats on there. And our duty was you did your watches with ship's company. Then you took care of your boat, make sure everything was right on it and cleaned; the life jackets was there; your guns were there; and clean the guns and all that kind of stuff you had to do. And then plus when they was under air attack, ship's company manned the guns. All the boat crews would stand by, like, I was, like, captain of the five-inch gun. If one of the guys got hit, then I would take over. Otherwise you stood by like that, because when you made invasion, you wasn't aboard ship no more.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How -- Did you have a lot of air battles, I mean, over here did you have a lot of air problems?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah. We had -- The biggest air was over in Okinawa when we was there. That's when we got the word they sending, like, three or four hundred kamikaze pilots there. And one of the ships traveled with us, they went right through their deck, right in the mess hall and everything. And then we had to send some boats over there to help finish unloading their ship and everything because they just knocked too many of the ship's company out of there, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was that the Merchant Marine?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: No. This was regular Navy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: It was?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: The one that got hit?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah. It was, like, troop transport, which carried 3,000 troops like our ship did. Same thing but just different name.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How many people got killed on that one?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Oh, there was about 50, I think, because they were having mess. That's where they hit the number five -- number three hatch. They hit in there. That was just above the conning tower -- not conning tower -- but the wheelhouse of the ship and everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So did you see these kamikazes?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: The what?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you see these kamikazes?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Oh, yeah, you could see them coming in, yeah. When they were coming in, they tried to strafe the landing craft, ___ boats in there, and everything like that, that plus the beach -- landing beach party was in there. You seen them constantly all the time, even in the Philippines when I was there and all that. They were -- Every invasion you'd see these air attacks, you know, but not too much kamikazes as it was in Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How many ships were laying off Okinawa? Lots of them?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, I would say about 20 mostly of destroyers and troop transports. You didn't see the battle wagons or the aircraft carriers. They were way out, you know. They could lob their shells all the way into the beach. But they had the destroyers in there protecting, you know, from submarine attacks, troop transports in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What was your most significant battle that you remember or --

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, you remember a lot of them, but when you know the war is coming in, Okinawa is the biggest, you know, for us, especially when we had word that we were returning to the states, you know, then. And then another one was at Palau, where you had to go through this channel, which I said before, the coral reef, you could go in there, but when the tide went out, you couldn't get in. So then they channeled all the boats in there, landing craft, right by ___ back, to unload them. Then you were there high and dry when it went out. So I spent about maybe four or five hours in there, you know, on the beach, which the battle was still going. So that was the scariest one, I think, where we had been there, had to do nothing, you know. And we didn't even have a side arm or nothing on us, just .30 calibers, which you couldn't shoot them, because you had troops in front of you, you know. But that was about the scariest, I think, of mine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Would you tell me when you got out, I mean, tell me -- We talked about the Magic Carpet. What was the Magic Carpet?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: The Magic Carpet is when we came back to the states to get an overhaul of the ship. They repainted it and everything. And then we -- It was in '45, because that's the year I got married up there, so my wife, we went to school together. And when we went back, I had troops on then. We got to Hawaii. And as we left Hawaii, the war -- they said the war was over. The Japs had surrendered. And these troops we had on all thought the ship was going to turn around and drop them off at the states. But they took them, like, on islands and dropped them off. And the Magic Carpet was we brought, like, Seabees and troops back that had been out -- veterans out there. And we brought them back. We made about three trips of that from out there to the states, you know. That's what that was, returning troops.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And when did you get finished?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: In the Navy?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Uh-hmm.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: I had -- I was in the regular Navy, so I did not get out until November of '46. I was in for -- They called it a kiddy crew, ___+ crews, because you went in when you was 17. But I should have got out in September of '46, but I had a, like, 60-day leave, and they just sent you home with that, you know. You're still, like, in the service, you know. And that's when I got out. But I did reenlist in --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: The Reserves?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Reserves, yeah. So when I went out, I stayed in there, and my time was almost up in the Reserves, and, as a matter of fact, it was almost up a month to go when I got called back in, and they extended me for about 18 months. So I've been to Korea and made one invasion there in Korea. And I was just lucky the ship -- excuse me -- ship I was on was rotated to come back to the states. And I also would like to mention my father. He, when I was stationed in Little Creek, he come and see me down there. Then I went through the Panama Canal. Who come aboard the ship, was my father again. Then out in the South Pacific, our landing craft boat went over, and they sent the word over, and I got to see my father out in the Pacific aboard his ship, which he, then, he was a chief warrant boatswain's mate. He got promoted to an officer then. So he retired out of the Navy. He had about 30 years in when he retired.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: He was in the Coast Guard originally?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, he was in the Coast Guard. He worked his way up to warrant officer there and got out. He used to catch rum runners in Florida. I don't know if you knoew about that, but they used to lay off the beaches in Florida and run the beach -- whiskey and booze in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So when did he get into the real -- yeah -- the real Navy? When did he get into the Navy?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: He went -- He enlisted in 1939.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: To the Navy?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah, right. And he went back in as first class petty officer and worked his way back up again to a warrant officer.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So before '39 he was already in? He was in the Coast Guard?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: No. He got out of that. Yeah, he went into Coast Guard in 1917.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah. He was, like -- He was born in 1900. So he had about a piece of the first war too, and he didn't get out. He -- Second war, Korean War, we were both together then. I'm not sure if he was in during the Vietnam War when he retired or not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, where was he stationed? How did you get here -- How did your family get here to Wilmington?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, he, when he got out of the Coast Guard, he moved to Dover. He had a farm down there. And then he sold that, and we moved in Richardson Park, Delaware. And from there we moved in Wilmington on East Fourth Street over -- people don't remember -- over the top of the commission houses there. They used to sell produce and stuff on Fourth Street there. And that's where he enlisted in the Navy in 1939.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Where was he stationed in the Coast Guard that you'd be in New Jersey? Was he down in Cape May or wherever --

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah, he was at Cape May, yeah, Cape May. And I think my brother was born in Florida. He was born at Fort Lauderdale down there. And I guess he was in the Coast Guard up in Michigan. That's where my sister was born, up in there. So we were born all over. So we had like what's called, like, what they call service brats or something like that, you know. That's why we moved around a little bit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me about all your family being in the service. Tell me about your brother and your sister and all that and your dad. Tell me how that all worked.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, my father enlisted in, so -- in the Navy, so as soon as I was 17, I went in, and went in, and after -- There's two years difference between me and my sister and my brother. My sister's two years older than me. I'm two years older than my brother. So I guess we all enlisted in, you know, all went into the Navy, you know. And my mother worked at Blanca out here making bomb bay doors. There was a Piper Cub air place out there or something out there in New Castle where she worked out there. So we all did a lot in the service, I would say. And that's why I really want this interview, because of -- show my family did their part in the second war and everything, you know. I'm very proud of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What did -- Your sister was in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah, she was in the WAVES, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What did she do, do you know?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: I, actually, I couldn't tell you. I couldn't tell you, because I was in the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was she a nurse or typist or --

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: No. I would say she was a clerk or something like that, you know, because she just came out, like, Seaman First. I couldn't even tell you how long she was in, because I was out in the Pacific most of the time, you know. My brother was out in the Pacific, too, but I never got to meet him out there. He was on an LST out there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was he a -- Now, the LST's had -- Hold on a second.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah, they carry them troops that go in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Hold on just a second.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: ____+ Lights. Do you see the light switches?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I'm just going to go ahead and if you could just come on over here -- oops, here we go -- just sit down here. We're almost finished with this interview. So we'll just -- All right.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: ___+ because they carried a lot of tanks on there. It was a pretty big ship. I couldn't tell you because I never was on one, you know. Like our ship, all right, we had ship's company was, like, 300, and we had about, ship's company and, like, small landing craft, we had about, like, 60 in there counting the officers in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: The LST's pretty much moved around on their own, right?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: They were full --

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah, they were pretty big --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What was the next one down, the next smaller one? It was about a 50-footer.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Oh, well, there was one LCT, I think it was called. They used to carry them on top of LST's.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Then --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You used to carry your boats inside those?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah. And then they used to have one on ours, was an LCM, landing -- We had four of them. They were 50-foot long, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That's what I'm thinking about.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah. We had four of them were there on the hatches. They would put another one on top of and carry it that way, whereas mine was on a davit, and they just lifted you over. As a matter of fact, when you made invasions, each hatch -- like you had four hatches where they carried the supplies -- they would lower the boats over the side. And the davits, they would lower them down, in case your ship got hit, they could get them away, you know, out of there, where if they lost their power and everything, so all they had to do was just drop them down, you know. So they were pretty well prepared how to make an invasion and everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: If you were to tell future generations about, what would you leave with them about World War II?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Well, it was something had to be done. Like I always tell people out here, I said, hey, the guys in the war did a great job, all of them. I want to say that, you know, women and everybody did a great job, to me. But, like I told them, if we didn't have that war and defended our country after they attacked Pearl Harbor, you might have all been slant eyes here or something, you know. So you've got to be proud of what the servicemen did and what they do today too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. When you got out, when did you join the Wilmington Fire Department? Tell me a little bit about that.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: I got out of the Navy in -- Like I said, I was under a 30-day leave, you know. So I went out -- These guys all went out to get a job, so I went with them, went out Blanca, went and got a job to sand and polish airplane wings there in September of '46. Then they closed down at the first of the year. You got your pink slip plus a turkey, you know. Then from there I knocked around jobs at the railroad. I worked there one day and got laid off of there. And then I worked at Bon Crown and Cork awhile, and I said I've got to get a job that's steady. So then I went to see this one guy I know was Mike Curl, and he was a captain on the fire department. I said I'd like to get on there and can I put your name down on my application. So I got called after the police investigated my background. So I went on there and put 20 years on there. And from there I moved to California for awhile. We came back again, my wife and I. And from there I went to Wilmington Medical Center, put 15 years in there, and retired out of there because I was 62, you know. And then from there I knocked around different places. Then I went to Happy Harry's. And I worked ten years there, moved to Florida and came back, and now I'm working for Happy Harry's now at a part-time job in the maintenance department. And I've just been lucky on jobs and things. So more or less it looks like I went to help people, I guess, after the war, you know, fire department, the medical center, and Happy Harry's, which, you know, drugs and things like that, so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Ask him.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: I have a question. When you haven't been there, it's difficult to think about how did you do an invasion? So I can imagine there's a whole fleet coming in shooting artillery, and then all your landing boats get assembled, and then there would be, what, one big wave? Is it like this?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah, they go in --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Look at me.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Oh, I'm sorry. Yeah, you went in there like on -- You circled on back of your ship until they called you in. See, you had a signalman, and they called you in. You loaded up your troops. Then you go out, and you made a circle, and you made a circle. They made different circles. They had signals. I can't remember what they were. You got in. Then you go into the beach, and you went in like the geese fly, you know, V-shape. And then when you got closer to the beach, they wave you out, and you spread out. That's the way you go into the beach. And then there would be another wave maybe 100 feet in back of you, you know. You dropped your troops off, and you got out of there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was it tough coming off of there sometimes?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Oh, sometime, yeah. But most of the times, because these troops got off, it lightened your boat up, so you got back off the sand, you know, pretty easy. But a lot of times you had a lot of waves. Some of the boats flooded in there. The waves come up over the top and flood them right out, you know, and everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Where was your navigation station? Was it in the center pretty much or -- You just had a wheel, right?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah. You just had -- You had that compass which you had to go by. They gave you what -- to go by, and then that's how you steered then. But most of them, they had the guide boats to show you where to go. Then they would peel off, you know, boat group commander. They would peel off, you know, and they wouldn't go into the beach. And then when you come back to your ship and you loaded up with certain supplies, you stopped by that boat group commander, and they'd tell you the position to go in, where to go, or they'd call you and say, okay, we want you to go into the beach for that supply, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you take the same troops back off as you put back on?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How did that work?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: We would never see the troop -- Also I would like to say is, like, our ship was a medi -- a hospital ship too. We had about 15 doctors we carried on there all the time, and that was, like, troops came back on there, you know, on there. They brought them back on. It was like a hospital ship, you know. And then they called the Hope, the big hospital ship, the real bad cases, they would send them over there, you know. So they had things pretty well organized when you hit the beaches and everything.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: So would you then shuttle the wounded people on demand?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Do what?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Would you shuttle --

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Would you shuttle the wounded? Tell me a little about that.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah. They give you the wounded to come back, yeah, to bring back the wounded. But you never brought the same troops back, no, just the wounded people, you know, because they stayed on invasion to shore there until they were properly relieved, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Who picked them up? How did they get out of there?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: I couldn't tell you. We never did that, you know. After you made your invasion, your ship was unloaded. Then they send you out of that, I guess, kind of air attacks, you know. They didn't want to get the ships hit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, when you were going from island to island with these invasions, where would you go pick your troops up?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: You'd pick them up at the different islands, yeah, different islands, wherever you went in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So for Okinawa, where would you pick your troops up to bring them into Okinawa, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: I'm trying to figure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you go back to Honolulu or --

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: No. Either, like, the Philippines or something. I'm trying to figure if it was the Philippines. ___+ Philippines, we went to Saipan, you know. I think we picked them up the Philippines, because when they made invasion of Okinawa, we had the troops aboard ship a good while, because I think that's when they hit Iwo Jima, and they, you know, they were getting the heck kicked out of them for a good while, and they didn't want to make another invasion until they may have had to use these troops for reinforcements in there, you know, so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And they were pretty much all Marine?

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Yeah. We made, I think, four invasions with the Marines and four with the Army. Four with the Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What were the Army ones? Because you don't hear too much about the Army ones.

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: No. They just made the same thing in there, you know, like the Marines on there, you know, just on the ship there, but they made invasions. I think most of them -- See, I made three invasions in the Philippines, and that may have been where we took the Army in the Philippines there, you know. As a matter of fact, I even got to see MacArthur when he landed in there, come in. My ship was there, you know, my boat was, laying off the beach, you know, when he came in. So that was pretty good seeing him. But I know he made people on the island feel happy that they were getting relief from the Japs in there.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Okay? ___+

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you want me to turn him in towards that, or do you want to do what?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: I think that's good ___+

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: He's just going to do some still shots of you right now, so you're just going to be still and --

sp.speaker: Harvey Parry
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. That didn't hurt.
